Patient demographics:

  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Hairdresser
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Photos): Related photos, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Khalid, a 38-year-old hairdresser of Middle Eastern descent, had always found solace in the vibrant colors and textures of his trade. His small salon in a bustling part of the city was a sanctuary for him, filled with the laughter of clients and the hum of hair dryers. However, everything changed when he received the diagnosis that would alter the course of his life: a severe, life-threatening illness that left him grappling with not only his health but also his sense of self and safety.

The day he learned about his illness was etched into his memory with vivid clarity. Sitting in the sterile examination room, the coldness of the walls and the clinical smell of antiseptics lingered in the air, suffocating him as the doctor delivered the news. The words “serious” and “treatment” echoed in his mind, twisting into something monstrous. From that moment on, Khalid’s world began to shrink. 

In the months that followed, Khalid found himself haunted by the specter of his diagnosis. The very thought of undergoing any medical procedure sent him spiraling. He avoided appointments, convinced that each visit would lead to more bad news or, worse, an uncomfortable procedure that would make him relive the trauma of his diagnosis. The sensation of being back in that examination room was so palpable that he could feel the sweat pooling in his palms and the tightness in his chest. He had come to believe that his body was betraying him, reacting as if danger was ever-present, even in the safety of his salon.

At night, Khalid’s sleep became a battleground. He would often wake from nightmares, drenched in sweat, his heart racing as he relived the moments of fear and vulnerability. Shadows from those dreams lingered in the corners of his mind, creeping into his waking hours. He would sometimes catch glimpses of photos from his past—snaps of joyous family gatherings or carefree outings with friends—and a wave of dread would wash over him. The visual reminders of happier times morphed into triggers, stirring emotions he had thought he had tucked away. What frightened him most was the realization that these moments of joy could now only remind him of what he had lost.

Khalid's daily life began to shift dramatically. He withdrew from social gatherings, avoiding friends who wanted to celebrate milestones or simply enjoy each other’s company. He told himself it was for their good, that he didn’t want to taint their happiness with his struggles. But as weeks morphed into months, the silence in his apartment grew louder, and the vibrant laughter of clients became a mere echo of what once was. The isolation weighed heavy on his heart, amplifying feelings of guilt and shame. He was ashamed of the fear that had taken residence in his chest, a fear that made him question his sanity. Sometimes, he felt as if he were going crazy, his body betraying him with its relentless tension and hyper-vigilance.

Memories of that life-altering moment would wash over him unexpectedly, igniting a visceral pain in his body that felt all too familiar. Khalid could almost smell the antiseptic from the doctor’s office, a scent that now triggered a physical reaction, a reminder of his vulnerability. It was as if his body was caught in a time loop, reacting to an invisible threat that only he could perceive. He could no longer trust his own body, which felt like an enemy rather than a vessel.

As Khalid sat in his salon one afternoon, the sunlight streaming through the window, he felt a flicker of hope. A client, noticing his withdrawn demeanor, gently asked if he was okay. The genuine concern in their eyes stirred something within him, igniting a tiny spark of courage. It was in that moment, amidst the familiar surroundings of his work, that he realized he could no longer bear the weight of his silence. He needed help. The thought of reaching out was terrifying, but the prospect of continuing to live in isolation was even more daunting. Khalid was both afraid and hopeful, hoping to reclaim not just his life, but his sense of safety and trust in his own body.
